title: Chasing Moving Targets with Online Self-Play Reinforcement Learning for Safer Language Models
claim: Safety improves when two opposing agents are trained against each other under a shared judge's reward in a zero-sum game.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right three nodes, return arrows below, min-max formula at bottom
description: A single wide diagram with three rounded-square icon nodes in a row: a red Attacker (boxing glove, labeled π_A) on the left, a green Defender (shield, π_D) in the middle, and a yellow Verifier (checkmark badge, r_φ) on the right. Black arrows run left to right: 'Prompt y_A' from Attacker to Defender, and 'Response y_D' from Defender to Verifier. Return arrows run from Verifier back to Defender, labeled r_φ(y_A, y_D), and to Attacker via a long curved arrow, labeled −r_φ(y_A, y_D). A min-max objective, min over y_A~π_A and max over y_D~π_D of r_φ(y_A, y_D), sits at the bottom. The eye goes first to the saturated red, green and yellow icons, then follows the arrows.
caption: Zero-sum red-teaming game. An attacker (πA) and defender (πD) compete under a verifier reward (rϕ) in a min–max objective that drives safety co-evolution.
abstract: Conventional large language model (LLM) safety alignment relies on a reactive, disjoint loop: attackers exploit a static model, then defenders patch exposed vulnerabilities. This sequential setup leads to attackers overfitting obsolete exploits while defenders perpetually lag behind emerging threats. To address this, we introduce Self-RedTeam, the first fully online self-play multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) algorithm that continuously co-evolves attacker and defender for robust safety alignment. A single policy self-plays as both attacker and defender, generating adversarial prompts and defending against them, with a reward model adjudicating outcomes. Each role uses hidden chain-of-thought for strategic planning. Grounded in two-player zero-sum game theory, we establish a theoretical safety guarantee: if the game converges to Nash Equilibrium, the defender produces safe responses against any adversarial input. Empirically, Self-RedTeam generalizes across five models from the Llama and Qwen families, uncovering more diverse attacks (+17.80% SBERT) and improving safety of RLHF-trained models by up to 95% across 14 benchmarks. Our work motivates a shift from reactive patching to proactive co-evolution, enabling LLM safety self-improvement via online self-play MARL. Link to code: https://github.com/mickelliu/selfplay-redteaming
